newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong leadership race heats up as Tung declares.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong leadership race heats up as Tung declares.

text.p: A billionaire shipping tycoon on Friday declared he was joining the contest to become Hong Kong's first leader after Britain hands the territory back to China next year.

The long-awaited annnouncement by magnate Tung Chee-hwa came as tensions simmered over China's attitude towards civil liberties in the territory, which will revert to Beijing's control at midnight on June 30, 1997.

Tung Chee-hwa, 59, ended months of speculation by resigning as chairman and chief executive of his family's shipping empire, Orient Overseas (International) Ltd, and by announcing he was entering the leadership race.
"During the last few months, I have met with social and political leaders from different sectors of society," he said in a statement.
"Their valuable opinions have enabled me to build a more comprehensive understanding and a more accurate grasp of Hong Kong's future challenges."
His move came a day after another unofficial candidate, lawyer Lo Tak-shing, said he was pulling out of the contest to succeed British Governor Chris Patten.
Businessman Peter Woo and Hong Kong's former Chief Justice, Sir Ti Liang Yang, are Tung's main rivals.
A former Appeal Court judge, Simon Li, said on Thursday he was considering whether to make a pitch for the top post.
The leader is to be chosen next month by a China-controlled 400-member Selection Committee now being formed, and not by universal suffrage.
Tensions between China and Britain have risen over remarks Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen made to the Asian Wall Street Journal this week.
Qian said Hong Kong should not be allowed to have protest demonstrations marking the anniversary of Beijing's June 4, 1989, anti-democracy crackdown.
"In the future, Hong Kong should not hold activities which directly interfere in the affairs of the mainland," Qian said in response to a question about the future of the protest rallies.
The remark caused shockwaves in this capitalist outpost of 6.2 million people. Many are already jittery about next year's takeover by China.
A Hong Kong government spokesman said on Thursday that London would press Beijing to clarify Qian's remarks. Hong Kong's democracy camp vowed to continue their annual protests.

In June tens of thousands of people turned out in Hong Kong to remember those who died in and around Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989. They staged a candlelight vigil, a ritual that has evolved into an annual tradition in the British colony.
Activists in the territory were disappointed that the three leading contenders for Hong Kong's post-handover leadership have dodged questions about Qian's comments.
"They aren't fit to be chief executive," pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau told Reuters on Friday. "They won't have the support of the Hong Kong people."
Lau said the candidates were afraid of upsetting Beijing's communist authorities who would have the ultimate say in their chance to be first Chief Executive under Chinese rule.
The campaign will heat up further after October 28, the deadline for nominations.
